title: Two-Mirror Angle Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you turn one mirror-angle dial and see how many images two mirrors make, and which angles give clean patterns.
pitch: The whole first screen is one dial and one ink colour: two hinged mirrors, a lopsided hand-drawn mark between them and the ring of its reflections. Drag the dial and watch the ring grow, snap shut at 60 or 45 degrees, and tear open at 70. You leave knowing why a kaleidoscope uses certain angles, why the textbook count of 360 over the angle minus one is only part of the story, and why an odd number of slices leaves a seam.
firstMinute: A page-sized picture already runs: the dial sweeps slowly from 90 to 45 degrees and the ring of reflections of a lopsided mark grows from 3 to 7 copies while a row of pips counts them. The visitor grabs the dial and drags it; at 60 degrees the ring closes with no gap and the dial clicks, which is the first success. No reading is needed, and the explanations sit below the picture.
conceptsToLearn: a mirror flips left and right
whyNow: Timeless; the constraint of one dial and a single ink colour is felt at once, and the page respects it for the whole lesson (extra controls live behind a More toggle).

purposeDetail.concept: Two plane mirrors hinged at angle theta make a ring of reflections. When 360 divided by theta is a whole number n, the n copies of the object (the original plus n minus 1 images) tile the circle exactly, every copy alternately flipped. That is the dihedral symmetry of order 2n that two mirrors at 180 over n generate. Other angles leave overlaps or gaps, and an odd n leaves a seam where two same-handed copies meet.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most coverage is a single exam formula (360 over theta minus 1) with the edge cases glossed over or stated inconsistently, so learners never see why the angle matters or what goes wrong when it does not divide 360.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious teenagers and adults, physics and geometry students, and makers who build kaleidoscopes.
prerequisites: knows what a mirror image is
can read an angle in degrees
misconceptions: Any mirror angle gives a pretty kaleidoscope pattern.
The formula 360 over theta minus 1 holds for every angle.
More mirrors always means more variety rather than a fixed set of tilings.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Turning the dial from 60 to 70 degrees: the ring that closed perfectly tears open, because the angle no longer divides the full turn; then at 120 degrees the ring closes but a seam appears that flips handedness, so the angle must divide a half turn for a seamless view.
demos: Hinge and glyph: drag the dial, see images appear and count them with pips
Snap angles: click through 90, 60, 45, 36, 30 and compare the count with 360 over theta minus 1
Off-divisor angles: set 70 or 100 degrees and see overlaps or a gap
Odd versus even slices: 120 and 72 degrees show the seam, 90 and 60 close; try a mirror-symmetric mark to heal the seam
More: move the object, then fold into the round tube view that makes the classic wedge pattern
checkQuestions: How many images do mirrors at 40 degrees make with the object centred?
Why does 100 degrees not give a clean ring?
Why does a mirror-symmetric mark hide the seam at 120 degrees?

research.summary: Two independent exam-prep pages state the image-count formula N = 360/theta - 1 with 60 degrees giving 5 and 45 degrees giving 7. University talk slides and a Rutgers article tie two hinged mirrors at pi/p to the dihedral group of order 2p. The edge cases (non-divisor angles, odd slice counts) are described inconsistently across sources, so the lesson derives them itself by exact unfolding geometry and tests the code against the verified values, labelling edge cases as the page's own derivation. The brief's constraint idea held up; the only thing I could not confirm is a strict even-only rule, which one patent contradicts (odd counts close if the mark is mirror-symmetric).

facts.claim: For two plane mirrors inclined at angle theta, textbooks and exam-prep pages give the number of images as 360/theta - 1 (as of 2026-10-14).
The same formula gives 5 images at 60 degrees and 7 at 45 degrees (as of 2026-10-14).
Two hinged mirrors at angle pi/p (180/p degrees) generate the dihedral group of order 2p (as of 2026-10-14).
Brewster Society analysis: for a general (non-divisor) angle the farthest images are ambiguous and depend on the exit mirror. Reported, not confirmed.
A patent says an odd segment count produces a clean ring only if the primary image is mirror-symmetric. Reported by one result, unconfirmed; the lesson derives this itself.
For angles that do not divide 360 some images overlap and the count is the integer part of 360/theta; sources are inconsistent on odd cases. Reported, unconfirmed.
Mirror-bounded triangles correspond to wallpaper groups p3m1, p4m, p6m (Dunham). Reported, unconfirmed; optional extension only.

design.coreLoop: Drag the dial, see the ring and the image count change at once, predict the next snap angle, then answer a check question and see the page confirm it with the picture; the surprise at off-divisor and odd angles keeps pulling the visitor back to test one more angle.
sophisticationHooks: Exact unfolding geometry (not just the formula) so non-divisor and odd cases are drawn truthfully
Handed mark that shows reflections as flipped copies in one ink colour using a hatched versus solid fill
Seam detector that highlights where two same-handed copies meet
Round tube view that turns the ring into the classic kaleidoscope wedge pattern behind More
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: SVG ring of reflections with one dial, snap points, image pips, odd/even seam demo, four check questions, intro and explainer text, pure tested geometry module. Cut: three-mirror wallpaper groups, sound, sharing.
risks: Edge-case rules (non-divisor counts, odd slice counts) are not consistently stated by sources; the page must present them as its own derivation, checked by node tests against the verified values 60 -> 5 and 45 -> 7, and show unverified claims as 'as of 2026-10-14, per <source>' or omit them.
The Brewster Society page could not be opened (host not found), so its claims stay unverified.
The single-colour constraint limits showing handedness; the hatched versus solid fill and a flip-marked glyph must be tested for legibility and contrast.
Search summaries blended results, so the independent-agreement marks rest on the separate result entries only.
